Max Ernst, the German-born Surrealist artist whose technical innovations and hallucinogenic imagery shaped the movement's visual language.

Born in Cologne, Ernst participated in post-war Dada before pivoting to Surrealism in the mid-nineteen twenties, where André Breton championed his work as exemplary unconscious expression. He created dreamlike, often nightmarish paintings populated by hybrid creatures, biomorphic forms, and apocalyptic landscapes reflecting psychological turmoil and historical anxiety. His palette remained earthy and disturbing.

Ernst invented frottage—taking rubbings of textured surfaces to generate automatic imagery—and grattage, scraping paint across canvas. These were methods to bypass conscious intention and access the illogical depths of the mind. More ideologically committed to Surrealist revolution than Salvador Dalí, he viewed the movement as a philosophical weapon against rationalism and conformity. He rejected art for pleasure.

Ernst pioneered collage techniques that anticipated postwar assemblage art. His enigmatic, poetic titles, often found or adapted, added another layer of interpretive slipperiness and automatic meaning. His insistence that accident and the uncontrolled mark reveal truth presaged postwar abstraction and Action Painting, making him a bridge between Surrealism and Abstract Expressionism.

During World War Two, Ernst survived in America. His late work remained deeply invested in primordial imagery and the eruption of unconscious material, positioning the artist as visionary shaman. He remained fundamentally devoted to the belief that artistic truth emerges not from rational control, but from the chaos of the unconscious mind.
